I've been using @media queries in CSS forever, but on a number of occasions these type of Viewport-only limits on width are problematic, especially in UIs that are user resizable or can otherwise dynamically change the sizing of components or panels.
My specific scenario is a resizable panel display where a fixed @media width causes problems due to the container, rather than the window, needs t resizing.

articles.description: A session cookie is a bearer token, which is a polite way of saying that whoever holds it is you. Copy the cookie, replay it from another machine, and the server happily serves your account. Nothing about the request proves which device it came from, so a cookie lifted by malware, an XSS payload, or a stray database backup keeps working until it expires. For a long-lived session, that can be weeks.
articles.title: Device Bound Session Credentials in ASP.NET Core

articles.description:
Anyone who has put a customer support agent backed by a large language model in front of real users has, sooner or later, watched it cheerfully write a Python web scraper or summarize last night’s football results, simply because somebody asked nicely. The usual remedy is to add a few more lines to the system prompt, asking the model to politely decline anything outside of its remit, however such approach means that every off-topic request still costs a full call to the support model, and that the very same model which is supposed to stay on topic is also the one deciding whether the request is on topic in the first place.
In this post we will look at a different arrangement, in which the scope decision is taken away from the support model altogether and handed over to Microsoft-Decision-1, a new model in Microsoft Foundry that does not generate any text at all, wired into a Microsoft Agent Framework agent as a piece of run middleware.
articles.title: Scope gating Agent Framework agents with Microsoft-Decision-1

articles.description:
Entanglement is fragile, and one of the more striking ways in which it is fragile was pointed out by Ting Yu and Joseph Eberly in 2004. Two qubits left to relax independently, each of them losing its excitation to its own environment, need not lose their entanglement gradually, the way the excitations themselves decay. Prepared in the state $\alpha|00\rangle + \beta|11\rangle$ with the doubly excited component the larger one, $|\beta| > |\alpha|$, they lose it completely at a finite time and it stays lost (for $|\beta| \leq |\alpha|$ it merely fades away), a phenomenon which Yu and Eberly named entanglement sudden death, and which was subsequently observed in a photonic experiment by Almeida and colleagues in 2007.
The reason it never comes back is, in fact, rather general. Once a state is…
articles.title: Sudden Death of Entanglement, Rebirth of Magic: Amplitude Damping in Q#

articles.description:
The no-cloning theorem is usually stated as an impossibility, namely that there is no machine which takes one copy of an unknown quantum state and returns two of them. The more interesting question, posed by Reinhard Werner in 1998 in a brilliant paper on optimal cloning, is the quantitative one, that is, how well we can produce $t+1$ copies of an unknown pure state when we are given $t$ of them. The answer for arbitrary states is rather sobering, since approximate cloning turns out to need as many copies as full state tomography does, which for $n$ qubits is exponential in $n$.
Modern quantum learning theory rarely deals with arbitrary states, however. It deals with structured classes, and for some of them learning is cheap. Stabilizer states are the canonical example, since an $n$-qubit stabilizer state can be learned from $O(n)$ copies. This raises the natural question of whether the structure that makes learning easy makes cloning easier still, and a recent paper by Nikhil Bansal, Matthias Caro and Gaurav Mahajan, Cloning is as Hard as Learning for Stabilizer States (arXiv:2604.15269, 2026), answers it in the negative, since the optimal sample complexity of cloning stabilizer states turns out to be $\Theta(n)$, the same as that of learning them.
In this post we shall implement the learner in Q#, run it on the QDK’s stabilizer simulator for up to 128 qubits, and measure the mechanism behind the paper’s lower bound, which turns out to be a single fact about random vectors over $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
articles.title: Cloning is as Hard as Learning - Stabilizer States in QDK & Q#

articles.description:
Hamiltonian simulation is the application for which quantum computers were originally proposed, and the question of how many gates it costs to simulate a given Hamiltonian to a given accuracy is one of the oldest in the field. For a long time the folklore has been that the accuracy dependence can be made logarithmic, since query-based methods such as qubitization and quantum signal processing reach an error $\epsilon$ with $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ queries to a block encoding of the Hamiltonian.
A recent paper by Alexander Zlokapa, Richard Allen and Aram Harrow (the last of whom is a towering figure in quantum algorithms, of HHL fame), Optimal Lower Bounds for Hamiltonian Simulation (arXiv:2607.19852, 2026), argues that for many physical Hamiltonians this is not what the gate count looks like. Unless one pays for every one of the terms of the Hamiltonian, the number of gates has to grow polynomially in $1/\epsilon$.
In this post we will take the central object of that paper, a cost function that says where a Hamiltonian should be cut between a deterministic and a randomized simulation method, implement the corresponding algorithm in Q#, and measure on a 6 qubit system whether the cost function predicts what actually happens.
